The route vector and both list node chains are engine-owned allocations that its allocator will eventually free, so a VirtualAllocEx substitute is a crash rather than the harmless leak that set_population.py accepts for the citizen vector. Rewriting the floats and ints INSIDE an engine-created order allocates nothing and is the safe way to retarget. A ship that has never been ordered reads 0 here: at game start three of four ships had 0 and only the one carrying a scout order had a pointer. SECOND INSTANCE (Aug 2026), an independently allocated COLONIZE order: 96 bytes again, heap header (0x66065B5A, 0x80001F00) at +96 with the UI status-bar string as the next block, so the size is confirmed twice on separately allocated objects. Route leg length matched the euclidean distance between its own endpoints exactly a second time (19.9755). The leg endpoints are consistently INSET from both ends: 2.04 from the ship's own position and 1.61 from the exact target, versus 1.6 on the scout order — so the engine plots orbit-edge to orbit-edge while +16/+20/+24 keeps the exact target. That makes the leg length SHORTER than the centre-to-centre distance, and external code that rewrites the leg with exact endpoints is therefore conservative (a slightly longer route, never a shorter one). +0 IS A ONE-BYTE BOOL: it read low byte 1 on both orders while the upper three bytes held 0x000000 on the scout and 0x632000 on the colonize order, i.e. uninitialised padding — the same 'read only the low byte' idiom as Owner:-12. +32/+36 and +56/+60 ARE NOT FIELDS: zero on the scout order but holding the ASCII fragments 'lect at ' and 'at the s' on the colonize one, which is residue from a freed UI string, not data. THE ENGINE NAVIGATES ALONG AN EXTERNALLY REWRITTEN ROUTE LEG — CONFIRMED by a pre-registered prediction. A colonize order was retargeted from one planet to another purely by rewriting +16/+20/+24 and the single route leg with EXACT endpoints (ship centre to target centre, length 40.9080), and one turn later the ship had moved 13.5000 units, exactly ShipDesign:36, directly along the new bearing. So the leg is authoritative input, not a cached derivative the engine recomputes. THE LEG INSET IS COLLINEAR WITH TRAVEL: the same turn, an engine-authored scout order displaced its ship 15.1321, which is precisely its 1.632 inset plus 13.5 of travel — the engine parks the leg origin slightly toward the destination (leaving orbit), so first-turn displacement is inset + speed rather than speed alone. Writing exact endpoints removes the inset and costs nothing but a marginally longer, i.e. conservative, route. +76 IS ROUTE PROGRESS — the distance travelled along the route so far, and it completes the movement model. A scout three turns into a journey read exactly 40.5 = 3 * ShipDesign:36 (13.5), and POSITION IS FULLY DERIVED FROM IT: leg_origin + route_unit_vector * progress reproduced the ship's live coordinates to an error of 0.000009. It also explains the ship's total displacement of 42.1320 as 40.5 of travel plus the 1.632 leg inset, so progress counts travel only and excludes the inset. CRITICAL FOR EXTERNAL WRITES: retargeting an order that has already travelled MUST zero +76, or the ship resumes from the inherited distance. Transferring a half-flown order without resetting it moved a ship 27.0 units in one turn at speed 13.5 — its 13.5 of stale progress plus one turn's travel — which presents as a speed bug rather than a stale field. ORDER OBJECTS ARE TRANSFERABLE BETWEEN SHIPS — PROVEN end to end: an order detached from one colony ship and attached to another, then retargeted, navigated correctly and founded the colony. Nothing is allocated or freed; the donor must be detached first so the object is never referenced twice. ORDER OBJECTS CAN BE ORIGINATED EXTERNALLY — CONFIRMED, and this removes the last blocker on driving ships without a user. The engine will not build one lazily and it cannot be fabricated, but it can be asked to build one: allocate 96 bytes with the game's OWN operator new at 0x0065165A (__cdecl, one argument, reachable directly from CreateRemoteThread since that passes exactly one stack argument), then run the game's OWN order constructor at 0x004E8420 on it. That constructor is __thiscall with SIX stack arguments, callee-cleaned — the count comes from its own ret 0x18 and was cross-checked against all 13 of its call sites, of which 0x00479685 shows six unobstructed pushes. Arguments are (ECX = the new block, origin object, target object, Owner, float, int 1, ptr 0). POINTER FORMS ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE: origin and target are ALLOCATION STARTS, i.e. EJBO tag - 8, which is why the constructor reads their coordinates at +0xc/+0x10/+0x14 rather than the +4/+8/+12 the tag-relative annotations use; the Owner must be its tag-52 primary form, which the game derives with lea reg,[node0-0x2c] from the tag-8 owner node at Ship:40. The float is whatever the ship's own vftable[0x30] getter returns (that getter takes no stack arguments, confirmed at two sites). VERIFIED IN GAME: a colony ship with Ship:48 null was given an order this way, the 3D view drew the route immediately and the ship moved correctly on the next turn. UI CAVEAT, cosmetic: the SHIPS TAB keeps showing the old command until a turn boundary passes, then catches up by itself. This applies to retargeted orders as well as constructed ones, and it is a deferred refresh of that list rather than anything wrong with the order — the engine acts on it the whole time. Tracked as a [ ] in the reconstruction report; it matters for multiplayer, where a player would not see server-pushed orders until the next turn. ROUT IS THE SAVE-BLOB FORM OF THIS OBJECT, AND THE ENGINE HAS A NON-UI CONSTRUCTION PATH FOR IT — read out of the binary, not yet checked against a real save blob. Writer Route::Write 0x004E5310, called from the ship writer at 0x0056ECC0; reader Route::ReadFields 0x004E6D40 via the factory 0x004E6E90, which allocates with operator new(0x60) — an INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION of the 96-byte size above, from the allocation site rather than from heap-block headers. On load the ship writer's counterpart peeks the next tag and, only if it is ROUT, builds the order and attaches it with Ship::SetOrder 0x004DA450, which stores it at ship_base+0x38 (= this annotation's +48) and, if the order's byte +0 reads 0, frees it again immediately and returns false. So a pushed order MUST carry a non-zero byte +0. ROUT is optional per ship: the writer skips it on a null order pointer (test ebx,ebx / je at 0x0056ECB9). Wire layout, in writer order, all little-endian, no per-field framing (the archive's WriteRaw at 0x005E5E10 is a plain memcpy append): u8 +0; u8 +1 (present only when the section version is >= 1, and the writer always emits version 1); f32 +4/+8/+12 origin XYZ; f32 +16/+20/+24 target XYZ; u32 count then count × 28-byte legs for the vector reached through +28; the same again for the vector reached through +52; f32 +76 progress; u32 +80/+84/+88; u32 = the object id behind the +92 reference node, or 0 when that node is empty. Fixed part 54 bytes, total 54 + 28 × (both leg counts). RESOLVES THE '+28 AND +52 ARE LIST HEADS' AND '+40/+44/+48 IS THE VECTOR' READINGS INTO ONE STRUCTURE: the writer passes +28 and +52 to the SAME helper 0x004E5200, which reads _Myfirst/_Mylast at +0xc/+0x10 of whatever it is given and divides the span by 28. So +28 and +52 are two objects OF THE SAME TYPE, each ≥ 24 bytes, each holding a 28-byte-element vector 12 bytes into itself — which is why the known leg vector sits at +40/+44/+48. PREDICTION, falsifiable and not yet tested: there is a SECOND leg vector at +64/+68/+72 (i.e. 12 bytes into the +52 object), holding the same 28-byte legs; on a live order (_Mylast - _Myfirst) there should be a multiple of 28. THE INTRUSIVE LIST NODES ARE NOT PERSISTED — the helper touches only the vector, and the reader constructs both +28 and +52 from scratch with 0x004A6D30 before filling them. That matters for injection: a pushed ROUT supplies leg vectors only, and the engine rebuilds the node chains that make this object unfabricatable by hand. ONE ASYMMETRY TO WATCH: the writer emits the reference id raw, but the reader ADDS the global at 0x00857C58 to any non-zero id before resolving it through the registry (0x004D9CA0), so injected ids may need to be written relative to that base rather than absolute. SAVE-BLOB SECTION FRAMING (read out of the archive class, supersedes the marker-scan in the recovered save_parser.py): every section, from the outermost SAVE down, has an 8-byte header of a 4-char tag followed by one u32 whose low 26 bits are the payload size EXCLUDING the header and whose top 6 bits are the section version. BeginSection 0x005E6260 writes the tag byte-swapped (which is why an MSVC multi-char constant lands as readable ASCII) with a 0x3FFFFFF size placeholder; EndSection 0x005E6320 patches the size in afterwards. Because the size is in the header the whole blob can be walked generically, and the old 'uint16 body_size + uint16 version 0x1000' reading of the SAVE header is that one u32 seen as two halves.

Owner:-44: CIV NAME — std::string SSO buffer, chars -44..-29. CONFIRMED: reads 'GoodGuy' on the human civ and 'BadGuy' on the AI, matching the names the UI shows on the diplomacy page. This is the player/civ name and it was invisible until the Owner read window was extended in front of the tag. Bytes past the length are stale buffer tail, not fields.
Owner:-28: Civ Name Length (std::string _Mysize) — 7 for 'GoodGuy', 6 for 'BadGuy'. A name longer than 15 chars would move the chars off-heap and make -44 a pointer instead; not yet observed.
Owner:-24: Civ Name Capacity (std::string _Myres) — 15 on both civs, i.e. the SSO buffer size. This is the field that identifies the struct as an MSVC std::string.
Owner:-20: Reads 0 on both civs and stable over time. Sits between the civ-name std::string (ends at -21) and the per-civ key at -16, so it is most likely padding or a reserved word rather than a field. No evidence either way
Owner:-16: PER-CIV KEY — a stable per-civ identifier, NOT a counter. CONFIRMED by finding its mirror: a two-word node [key, Owner*] exists for each civ (0x0A525A80 for GoodGuy, 0x0A5257A0 for BadGuy), and these are nodes of an MSVC std::map whose head is at 0x02D48740. Walking that tree enumerates EXACTLY the live civs, with each node's key equal to that civ's -16 value. So this is the key of the OWNER REGISTRY — see the report section on creating a third player. Value looks like a hash (0x2DB018D6 / 0x6C157D63) and its origin is unknown, which matters: a fabricated civ needs a key that does not collide
Owner:-12: A ONE-BYTE BOOL, value 1 on both civs — the upper three bytes are UNINITIALISED PADDING, not part of the field. This offset reads 0x02E44501 on the human civ, and 0x02E44500 really is the address of a live SolarSystem object, which makes 'tagged pointer to the home system' look compelling. It is wrong: the AI civ reads 0x00000001, i.e. a null pointer, and the AI certainly has a home system. MSVC writes a bool as a single byte and leaves the adjacent three untouched, so the human's 45 E4 02 is residue from whatever occupied that allocation before. Read ONLY the low byte here. What the flag means is unknown; it is 1 on both civs

ShipDesign:260: OWNER LINK — CONFIRMED, and it is the field that decides whether a design belongs to a civ at all. Reference node whose node[0] is the Owner, the same idiom as Ship:40 and Planet:40. Read across four designs and two civs: both 'Colony Ship' designs resolved to their own civ, and two designs created through the UI resolved to the civ that made them, while a design built externally by calling the engine's default constructor carried the static null node 0x00857C54 instead. So the default constructor does NOT set an owner; the design editor does. This is the leading explanation for an externally constructed design being absent from the UI's design list despite existing, being EJBO-tagged and being enumerable by a memory scan. WRITABLE: pointing it at a node taken from another design of the same civ is a plain pointer write with no allocation. Take the node from an existing design rather than fabricating one, for the same reason Ship:40 requires it.
